source.title: Findings of the BabyLM Challenge: Sample-Efficient Pretraining on Developmentally Plausible Corpora
source.authors: Alex Warstadt; Aaron Mueller; Leshem Choshen; E. Wilcox; Chengxu Zhuang; Juan Ciro; Rafael Mosquera; Bhargavi Paranjape; Adina Williams; Tal Linzen; Ryan Cotterell

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates downstream benchmark performance across different pretraining-data budgets and reports scores, but does not measure held-out cross-entropy loss or fit scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The paper cites quantitative scaling laws but does not test them. Its own results concern benchmark scores, including comparisons between Strict-Small and Strict data budgets and large pretrained skylines; these bear on V6, not on loss power laws, extrapolation, compute-optimal allocation, or loss-shape claims. The reported multimodal benchmark results do not test whether power-law loss scaling holds in other modalities.
record.test_reason: In a small-data setting (10M vs 100M words), the study reports downstream benchmark scores for the same OPT-125M baseline at two data budgets. It also compares submissions and skylines across data scales. This bears weakly on V6, the direction of downstream gains with data. It measures no loss, fits no curves and has only two controlled data points, so V1–V5 and V7 are untested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is partly right but misses the main conclusions. The authors conclude that data-efficient training choices dominate: the LTG-BERT-based winners outperformed Llama 2 trained on trillions of words, and architecture changes, preprocessing (short sequences), distillation and many epochs helped. Curriculum learning largely failed and multimodal input did not reliably help. More data (Strict vs Strict-Small) helped baselines clearly, but submissions only modestly. No conclusions about loss scaling laws are drawn.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses benchmark task scores from a community challenge with different models and training setups; it does not reproduce the original held-out-loss scaling measurements or fit scaling laws.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that benchmark performance varies with data budget, architecture, training objective, preprocessing, and hyperparameter choices; GLUE evaluations include fine-tuning for submissions and in-context learning for Llama 2.

fits_no_version.finding: Training for many epochs over fixed 10M/100M data (up to 200–2000 epochs) kept improving benchmark scores in several submissions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Repeated epochs over a small fixed corpus continue to improve downstream performance far beyond typical epoch counts.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the BabyLM Challenge at the 27th Conference on Computational Natural Language Learning
record.problems: No held-out pretraining loss or scaling-law fits; no controlled sweep over parameter count, tokens, or compute; comparisons span heterogeneous architectures and training procedures. Scores have no reported uncertainty in the cited tables, and GLUE evaluation procedures differ for Llama 2 and challenge submissions.

untested.parts: No held-out loss or power-law fits.
Architecture strongly changes benchmark scores, but loss at fixed parameter count is not measured.
Multimodal and repeated-data submissions report benchmark scores only, with no scaling form.
Untested: predictability from pretraining loss, any functional form, and sweeps beyond two data budgets.

missing.what: MSGS scores for the OPT-125M baseline, Strict-Small vs Strict: aggregate 0.10→0.13 (a weak gain) and macro MCC -0.45→-0.39. The text says more data helps MSGS but 'not always'.
BLiMP skyline comparison: RoBERTa-base 0.87 vs Llama 2 0.84. The text says bigger models are not better on BLiMP 'as a rule'.
Top submissions vs Llama 2 skyline: ELC-BERT aggregate 0.74 (Strict, 100M) and 0.66 (Strict-Small, 10M) vs Llama 2 0.71.
Across-submission Strict vs Strict-Small comparison: the gains are small, with only two Strict models beating the best Strict-Small GLUE.

record.verdict_notes: Shared-task findings paper, not a scaling study. The only controlled scale contrast is the baseline at 10M vs 100M words. GLUE is fine-tuned for challenge models but uses in-context learning for Llama 2. Evaluation sets are vocabulary-filtered, so scores are not comparable to standard benchmarks. No uncertainty is reported.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss measurements or power-law fits over parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run loss fits are used to predict much larger-run losses.
No fixed-compute comparison or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation is measured.
Architecture and benchmark comparisons are discussed, but the study does not measure loss changes from varying depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Multimodal submissions are summarized using benchmark scores, not loss scaling laws across modalities or regimes.
The study reports benchmark performance across data budgets and models, but does not test predictability from pretraining loss or provide a controlled, broad scale sweep.
No scaling-law exponents or compute-optimal splits are fitted or compared across setup choices.

relationships.condition: Same OPT-125M baseline recipe, 10M vs 100M words
relationships.reason: BLiMP, GLUE, BLiMP-Supplement and aggregate all rise with 10x data (r2, r4, r6, r8). The direction is consistent, but only two points.
relationships.display_finding: Increasing training data from 10M to 100M words improved BLiMP, GLUE, BLiMP-Supplement and aggregate performance.

relationships.condition: Across architectures and training recipes (submissions and skylines)
relationships.reason: Based on the text, since rows mostly do not capture this. Strict submissions barely beat Strict-Small (only two beat the best Strict-Small GLUE). LTG-BERT at 100M beats Llama 2 (2T tokens) on aggregate. RoBERTa beats Llama 2 on BLiMP. MSGS does not always improve with data. Data scale alone does not predict downstream rank (r9, r10 confounded).
relationships.display_finding: Only two Strict submissions exceeded the best Strict-Small GLUE score, LTG-BERT at 100M tokens beat Llama 2 at 2T tokens overall, RoBERTa beat Llama 2 on BLiMP, and MSGS did not consistently improve with more data.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: OPT-125M baseline, Strict versus Strict-Small track scores
reader_labels.reason: The reported BLiMP, GLUE, BLiMP-Supplement, and aggregate scores are higher for Strict than Strict-Small (r1-r8), consistent with better benchmark performance with more pretraining data in this comparison.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: The reported data-budget comparison and skyline model comparison
reader_labels.reason: The paper says Strict models did not outperform Strict-Small models by a large amount overall, and only two Strict models exceeded the best Strict-Small GLUE score; skyline comparisons also vary architecture and evaluation procedure, so the results do not establish predictable performance scaling (r1-r10).
